WebGL confirmed: a full-viewport (1440x900) canvas with a live getContext('webgl') present at nearly every station — most likely the source of the page-wide, near-invisible grain/dither reading that shows up as tiny ambient percentages (0.3-2%) across huge swathes of the frame from the mid-page onward. Rive confirmed at the DOM level: individual canvases at multiple stations report data-rive attributes (small 50x50/37x37/73x63/81x43 nav-icon-sized canvases plus one 800x571 canvas on the hero) even though the page-wide heuristic check (querySelector for canvas[data-rive]) came back false — the per-canvas attribute check is the more reliable of the two and is what surfaced the cursor-tracked wireframe-helmet HUD. No <video> element anywhere on the homepage and no <audio> — despite feeling cinematic, this whole experience is built from stills, canvas/WebGL, and scroll-driven transforms, not footage. No dedicated custom-cursor element (nothing matching a 'cursor' class); the wireframe helmet effectively does that job instead. A persistent full-viewport div (class 'transition-w') is present, sticky/fixed and covering 100% of the viewport, at literally every station from y=0 to y=13500 — but no station's screenshots showed a frozen/stuck viewport, so this is almost certainly an invisible page-transition curtain for client-side route changes (e.g. to /on-track), not a scroll-jacked pin. Notably, document.getAnimations().length returned exactly 0 at every single station with no exception — none of this site's motion runs through the native Web Animations API or CSS transitions; it is all imperative, driven by WebGL/Rive/rAF, which is exactly why a naive "how many animations are running" check reads as zero on a page that in practice never stops moving.

deep.alwaysMoving: The heart of it is one fixed, full-viewport Three.js (r174) WebGL canvas ("data-engine":"three.js r174" on a 1440x900 canvas.gl in .gl-wrap) that appears to sit through the whole page: it is the source of the wavy topographic contour-line backdrop visible behind almost every section, and it drifts continuously and independently of scroll and mouse — confirmed by parking the headless mouse at (0,0), taking 5 frames over 2s at every section, and diff-heatmapping f0 vs f4: the diff pixels trace the contour lines exactly, nothing else. That gives the whole site a constant low hum (~1-2% frame delta every 500ms) even on "static" sections. Layered on top of that hum are three louder, TIERED sources of motion, none of them idle CSS loops: (1) the hero's periodic glitch — over a dense 7s/300ms sample, diffs cycle from ~1-2% up to ~14% and back with a ~3.3-3.6s period: for ~1.2-1.5s, 3-4 diagonal bands tear across Lando's static portrait revealing a McLaren-branded helmet/visor photo underneath, then it calms for ~1.8-2s to just a translucent 3D wireframe dome (the Three.js object) drifting near his head trailing a small checkered marker; (2) two literal marquees — a WebGL-rendered opposing-type ticker behind the "message from Lando" video block, and a horizontal partner/sponsor-logo row in Collabs and the footer — both are canvases (class names like "marquee-gl-target" return transform:"none" in the DOM because the motion happens inside the canvas, not as a DOM transform) scrolling continuously at a steady ~7-8% delta every 500ms with no settle; (3) one-shot Rive state-machine plays triggered by scroll-into-view rather than looping — Lando's signature drawing itself in (file "signature", state machine "signature_play", once in the marquee block, once small in the footer) and the hand-drawn loop/scribble behind "PARTNERS & CAMPAIGNS" (file "phrases", artboard "collabs", state machine "page_home") — both finish and hold, they do not re-loop at rest.

(3) THE SIGNATURE — a Rive-drawn scribble (state machine "signature_play") shown large in the marquee block and small under quotes/the footer headline; same stroke path, just rescaled. (4) THE McLAREN LAUREL + "MCLAREN F1 SINCE 2019" LOCKUP — a fixed, always-centered, always-static chapter-marker opening the hero's NEXT RACE widget, the marquee's video block, the intro headline, and the open nav menu's footer. (5) THE LIME ACCENT + "L7" LOGOMARK — the nav wordmark's compact glyph, the STORE pill, every CTA, every hover/mask color — the one constant color thread stitching the black-on-cream sections to the dark-olive ones together.
deep.typeMotion: Two distinct systems, not one. (A) BLOCK-WIPE MASK — the site's real signature move: a lime (or background-matched) rectangle sits over not-yet-revealed words and slides away to expose them. Used on the "REDEFINING LIMITS, FIGHTING FOR WINS..." headline (scroll-scrubbed — tied to scroll position, so it visibly holds mid-reveal if you stop scrolling mid-section, not a play-once-on-enter), the "See more helmets..." CTA line, every label inside the open nav menu (MCLAREN F1 SINCE 2019, BUSINESS ENQUIRIES, each social link), and the body-copy lines in the post-OTOT editorial block. All of these share one declared CSS token — 0.75s, cubic-bezier(0.65,0.05,0,1) (the site's global --duration-default/--cubic-default) — though most resolve visually faster (~300-400ms) because that curve front-loads almost all of its motion. (B) LIVE MARQUEE TYPE — a WebGL-rendered ticker (an actual <canvas>, "marquee-gl-target" — its DOM element reports transform:"none" because the motion happens inside the canvas, not as a CSS transform) mixing an olive serif line with a bold cream sans line, both scrolling continuously and independently of scroll position — a genuine idle loop, not scroll-scrubbed, holding a steady ~7-8% frame delta every 500ms with no settle. Numerals (event-photo years, "2025"/"2024" captions, the "#1"/champion marks) are static — never scrubbed or counted-up. The kinetic budget is spent entirely on the two systems above, not on numerals or body copy in general.
deep.phone: Nearly everything survives, restaged for touch, at 390x844 (isMobile/hasTouch). The hero's ambient layer is intact — an 8-frame/400ms pixel-diff sweep still shows ~4-10% motion — but mobile adds an explicit "TAP TO LOCK" prompt with a hand-cursor icon bottom-right of the hero, implying the floating wireframe/glitch trigger is otherwise driven by device orientation or touch-drag on mobile and needs an explicit gesture to freeze, since there is no ambient mouse to drive it passively — this is the "what replaces hover" answer for the hero specifically. The horizontal-scroll moodboard is fully retired on mobile: it becomes a plain vertical stack of the same captioned photos, an honest simplification rather than a cramped fake-swipe carousel. The helmet grid drops from a dense multi-size bento to a clean 2-column grid, keeping the notched-corner card style. The hamburger menu keeps its clip-path ellipse blob-open and the lime block-wipe label reveals (caught mid-wipe on "M[CLAREN F1 SINCE 2019]" and the social row) but drops the 4-photo bento entirely (no room) and shrinks the McLaren lockup. The footer runs the exact desktop recipe — same SVG-masked rounded-top room, giant helmet, Rive signature, sponsor-logo marquee. What's unconfirmed: every hover-dependent moment (helmet-card image swap, STORE text-roll, CTA icon-rotate) has no observed touch/tap equivalent in this pass — they may fire on tap-and-release, which a static capture sequence can't distinguish from an ordinary click-through, so I'm not claiming they're absent, only that this pass didn't catch a replacement gesture for them.
deep.assetsVsSystem: The wow-factor splits cleanly into a reusable engineering layer and bespoke assets riding on it. SYSTEM (portable to any brand/assets): a single fixed, full-viewport Three.js r174 canvas (confirmed via a data-engine attribute on a 1440x900 canvas.gl inside .gl-wrap) that appears to drive the topographic contour-line backdrop drifting continuously site-wide, independent of scroll or mouse; a fleet of small Rive state-machine canvases supplying nearly every discrete micro-interaction (file "btn-ui"/artboard "arrow" on every CTA icon; artboard/state-machine "hamburger" on the menu button; file "phrases"/artboard "collabs" on the partners-section doodle; file "reef"/artboard "off-icons" on a small social icon; file "signature" for the hand-signature draw-in); the lime block-wipe text-mask technique (pure CSS clip-path + the global 0.75s cubic-bezier(0.65,0.05,0,1) token) used for every headline/label; the WebGL marquee-ticker technique; the nav's [data-nav-theme] light/dark auto-recolor as sections change background; and the footer's SVG clip-path "room" mask. None of that requires Lando's face, helmets, or footage to function — it would look identical wrapped around a logo, a phone screenshot, or plain type. ASSET-DEPENDENT: the payoff of nearly every one of those systems is Lando-specific content — the hero's glitch reveals a real McLaren-branded helmet/visor photo; the helmet-card hover swap only works because a matched studio+action photo pair exists for all 12 helmets; the moodboard needs dozens of curated event photos; the signature is literally his handwriting; the "message from Lando" block implies a video only a real person can supply. The honest takeaway for a client build: license the same motion recipes (a Three.js ambient backdrop, Rive micro-icons, clip-path block-wipe type, a WebGL ticker) and they will genuinely transfer — but a real photo/video shoot is still required to fill the payoffs; the technology alone can't manufacture the "that's clearly him" moments that make each system land.

gap.rootCause: Your site doesn't move less than Lando's. It moves the same amount. When you scroll, about 20% of the screen changes on both sites (20.2% on his, 19.8% on yours), and your work rail's biggest moment (49.8%) is about as big as his biggest (52.9%). The difference is when things move, what moves, and whose it is. On his site something keeps moving even when you stop scrolling: the thin wavy lines behind everything drift on their own, words run past behind his photo, and a strip of logos rolls under the partners and again along the bottom of the footer. You catch that at 16 of 31 stops, spread from the top of the page to the bottom. On yours, after the first two screens, everything stops the moment your hand stops, for 26 stops in a row (78% of the page). Next, Lando's words never move once they've landed. They wipe in one time and then hold, and the movement happens behind and around them. And everything that moves is his: his face, his helmet, his signature. Even the wavy background lines are the same swirl that's printed on his helmet and his jacket. On yours, the headline itself swaps words on a timer, and the soft glow behind it could be on anyone's site. The main reason, though, is this. His site was designed once, by one studio, as one character. Yours was built one section at a time, and each section came from a different site you loved. The title rise, the big poster and the work rail came from leoparpeix. The rotating word, the paragraph beat and the tile slot came from Huge. The bento and the blur-in title came from Apple, the card recede and the corner switch from Off+Brand, and the film placement from Cosmos and Clay. Each one is good by itself, which is why you liked each one. Side by side, though, they move in different ways, so the page reads as a collection instead of one person. Another reference or more animation won't fix this. The fix is to pick EAS's own version of the helmet: one pattern and one object that belong only to you (the EA mark, the real sites and phones you ship, and you). Then run Lando's quiet always-moving layer and one way of moving text through the whole page.

concepts.theSystem:
THE RULE: motion belongs to the ground and to the objects. It never belongs to the words. Five clauses generate every section's motion.

(1) ONE GROUND. A fixed layer draws the contour lines of a single terrain. The terrain is the EA mark's signed-distance field laid out 2.6 screens wide (so the lines run in the mark's rounded right-angle bends and its one long diagonal), plus slow hills on top. It never stops. The hills drift on time at about 2–4px/s, which matches Lando's measured 1–2% of the frame per 500ms (deep pass). The page travels over it at 1:10 of scroll, Lando's hero-image parallax ratio (decodes §10). It is drawn one tint off the ground. I measured Lando's contour cores today from lando-deep/ambient-*: +10 median / +17 core on his dark olive, −15 / −31 on cream. So the lines sit at about +13 levels on the void and −20 on paper. This is the only thing on the page that is always moving, so being alive at rest has one source, and that source is EAS's own geometry. His lines are his helmet's swirl; ours are the mark's offsets.

(2) SECTIONS DECLARE; THEY DON'T ANIMATE. Each section sets three numbers on the existing scroll engine: ink (how much ground shows), drift (how fast the clock runs under it) and lamps (whether light falls on it). One resolver, walking the page in document order, blends a section's values in as its top crosses 1vh → .5vh, eased 2t−t² (Lando's measured flip curve, decodes §2). Colour-like values snap; nothing else chases. This is Lando's data-gl-change-from/to: his Partners section literally declares its contour ink away, from tint to white (grammar §2.13). So loud sections turn the ground down and quiet ones turn it up. Motion takes turns (principle 2): the ground is loudest in the back third, where Lando has 7/10 stops moving on their own.

(3) LIGHT IS THE ONLY ACCENT ON IT. The cursor is a lamp on the lines, taken from landoGL.params.backgroundScene: cursor colour #b2c73a, CURSOR_INTENSITY .15 (grammar §2.16). It is not a glow that slides. The room's existing lamps, the film's edge light and the voices' --lit become light that falls on the lines. Cyan appears on the ground only where light is.

(4) THE WORDS LAND ONCE AND HOLD. There is one triggered vocabulary (data-wipe at top 90%, once — laws 3/11). Nothing inside a sentence runs on a timer. The only type that moves lives in the ground's own ink: two ticker rows under the film and one live-domain strip, mid-page and again at the foot. These are Lando's two strips: the ticker behind his portrait and the partners/footer logos.

(5) THE GROUND TURNS THE CORNER ONCE AND COMES HOME. It switches axis with the work rail, the page's one sideways move (law 10), and changes colour once across it with `paper` (law 2, the census 3,000px ramp). At the close it converges on the lockup's mark, and the mark writes itself on the same scroll. The terrain you crossed for 14,000px was the mark. Lando's GL layer resolves into his helmet on his head; ours does it once, as the bookend (law 12).

Everything except the drift is derived: travel = f(scroll), section weight = f(scroll), light = f(cursor, --lit), homecoming = f(scroll). Time drives only the drift, because time is the one input that means "this is alive right now".
concepts.whyItWowsWithoutStealing:
It moves where Lando moves, under everything and all the time, and nowhere he doesn't.

(1) It fills the exact hole the census measured. Today EAS has 26 dead stops in a row (78% of the page) and 5/31 stops moving on their own, all in the first 1,800px. The ground breathes at every stop: the target is ≥16/31 moving on their own, with ≥4 in every third. It does this at Lando's own amplitude, one tint off the ground and 2–4px a second. That is below the level where it competes with a word, and above the level where a page reads as dead.

(2) Nothing touches the message. Words land once and hold. The rotating word and the crossfading captions (the two frames where the census caught two messages on top of each other) stop moving. Moving type exists only as engraving in the ground's ink, never inside a statement. That is Lando's split: the ticker behind the portrait, the statement still.

(3) It is EAS's own, not atmosphere. Every line is an offset of the EA mark: rounded right-angle bends and one long diagonal that no other site can draw. It is to EAS what the swirl is to Lando's helmet and jacket. The page pays it off at the end: the terrain collapses onto the lockup and the mark writes itself. That is a whole surface moving, the "dramatic" Jake has defined. It happens at tint level, so it reads as mood rather than an event, like Lando's 3,000px ramp.

(4) It turns the collage into one character without rebuilding a section. The same ground runs under leoparpeix's poster, the bento, Huge's paragraph, the rail and the Off+Brand ending. It turns up, down, lights and corners by declaration, so the page reads as one studio's system. This is the root cause the gap analysis named. Adding a ninth reference couldn't fix it.

(5) It gives Lando's three rates per viewport (content 1:1, pictures' parallax, ground 0.1) without moving a single piece of content.

(6) It costs about 1ms of GPU and no main-thread paint. The room has twice measured paint-bound effects (the flip, the word colour-mix) failing at 13.6ms/frame; this avoids that failure class.

concepts.tech:
It needs WebGL, and I've weighed that honestly. The installed stack can't do it well:
- Animated SVG feTurbulence, or a canvas-2D marching-squares field, repaints the full viewport on the CPU every frame. That is the same paint-bound class this room already measured failing: 13.6ms/frame on the flip, 13.8ms on the per-word colour-mix.
- A pre-rendered SVG contour sheet with a transform drift is cheap, but it can only slide rigidly. That reads as "the whole background moving" (Jake, 2026-09-22). Lando's diff heatmaps show lines changing shape in place.
- A fragment shader draws per-pixel contour lines of a changing field for about 1ms of GPU and almost no main thread.

No library. Lando uses three.js r174 because he renders a 3D helmet, which EAS doesn't want (decodes §8). We draw one full-screen triangle: raw WebGL2 with a WebGL1 fallback, about 250 lines and ~5KB of our own code.

Architecture (grammar §2.16 / decodes §11):
- An empty fixed anchor holds one canvas: z-index 1, before .dr-grain so the grain and vignette sit over it, pointer-events none, aria-hidden.
- It boots in requestIdleCallback about 450ms after first paint. A canvas is never LCP.
- DPR is capped at 1.25 (Lando's measured cap). It draws at 60fps while scroll or the cursor move and 30fps at rest. It stops on visibilitychange and wherever the resolved ink is 0.
- The mark's SDF is computed at boot from the path D already in mark-svg.tsx: a 512² offscreen fill plus a 2-pass Euclidean distance transform, about 8ms, no network. It is uploaded as one RG8/R16F texture.
- Inputs come from scroll-engine.ts: a new field resolver (data-field-ink / -drift / -lamps, ONE writer in document order, decision 49's lesson) and a small shared store (Lenis animatedScroll, the rail's x and pinned distance, --flip, the lockup rect). The canvas reads the store in its own rAF; Lando runs 8–10 small loops.
- Tickers and strips are DOM, not GL: JS-written translate on 4 clones (decodes §6), with will-change: transform on the tracks only (decodes §11 rationing).

Fallbacks:
- No WebGL, a lost context or Save-Data: a baked static SVG of the field at t=0 (same SDF, built by a Node script), moved at 0.1× scroll by the engine.
- prefers-reduced-motion: time frozen, one redraw per declared change, tickers still, no homecoming zoom.
- Touch: the cursor lamp sits at the last touch point and fades over 1.2s. Everything else is the same; Lando keeps his ambient layer on phones (deep pass).
- No parting of lines around text: Lando's lines run straight under his type (the glyphs visibly interrupt them in lando-deep otot-home). Legibility comes from tint contrast, not geometry, which also keeps the canvas free of per-frame rect reads (decisions 67/68).
concepts.firstStep:
Build THE GROUND alone, behind `?v=survey` (a trial token added to the default set; no defaults change until Jake sees it).

(1) Create components/dark/survey.tsx, a client component mounted once in hero-room.tsx just before `.dr-grain`. It is an empty `position:fixed; inset:0; z-index:1; pointer-events:none` anchor holding one `<canvas aria-hidden>`. Export `D` from components/room/mark-svg.tsx and import it.

(2) Boot in requestIdleCallback after first paint (setTimeout 450ms fallback). Get a WebGL2 context (alpha, premultipliedAlpha, antialias:false; WebGL1 fallback). Build the mark SDF: fill D into a 512×512 OffscreenCanvas with the 500-unit box inset 6%, run a 2-pass Felzenszwalb EDT inside and outside, store signed distance in mark units, LINEAR filter. Outside the texture, d = texD(clamp(q)) + length(q − clamp(q)).

(3) Write the fragment shader over one full-screen triangle:
- For each pixel, P = fragCSSpx + (0, 0.1·scrollY), using Lenis animatedScroll (1:10, decodes §10).
- q = (P − origin)/M·500, with M = 2.6·max(vw, .75vh) (3744px at 1440×900). Place the origin so the first screen sits on the E's top-left rounded corner.
- h = dMark(q)·M/500/I + 1.6·fbm2(P/620px + t·(.021, −.013)), with I = clamp(34px, 3.3vw, 56px) (48px at 1440).
- line = 1 − clamp(abs(fract(h+.5)−.5)/fwidth(h) − .5, 0, 1): 1 CSS px, antialiased.
- Colour: white at α .055·ink on the void, black at α .09·ink under .dr-day.
- Cursor lamp: a gaussian of radius 200px adding α .10, tinted 50% toward --accent, position chased .08/frame, ×1.5 while over a or button.
- The three existing lamps (their 23/29/19s clocks and positions) become +α .06 pools.
- DPR = min(devicePixelRatio, 1.25).

(4) Drive it from its own rAF. Draw every frame while scrolling or while the pointer moves, every second frame at rest. Stop on visibilitychange. Time advances by dt × resolved drift, so a section slows the clock and never jumps it. Add the resolver to scroll-engine.ts: sections carry data-field-ink / -drift / -lamps, and one pass in document order blends each section's values in as its top crosses 1vh → .5vh on 2t−t², unchased. Declare (ink/drift): hero .8/1; band 1/.8; §02a .45/.5 with lamps off; show .6/.3; §02b .8/.7; tiles .3/.3; work 1/.25; voices 1/.8; runs and objections 1/1; close 1/.8. Under the token, do not bind .dr-atmos's quickTo parallax.

(5) Reduced motion: time frozen, redraw only on declared changes. No WebGL or context lost: hide the canvas; the baked still is step 2.

concepts.name: THE SCREEN: EAS's helmet
concepts.oneLine: Everything EAS shows is shown on one object, the Screen the hero film plays in, and in every section it is the only thing that moves. It plays, becomes three, travels the rail, carries the clients' words, steps back, and comes home at the close signed by the mark writing itself.
concepts.theSystem:
THE RULE: one object carries the page, and in any section that object is the only thing that moves on scroll.

The object is THE SCREEN, the window the hero film plays in. Two reasons it is the right object:
- It is what EAS actually makes: a site on a screen.
- It is the one moving thing EAS already owns. The census calls the film the page's best moving moment, and "motion that is the deliverable is Lando's hero exactly".

It is Lando's helmet. His helmet is restaged at every scale with a different livery (14+ liveries photographed identically). Ours is the clients' real sites on one identical frame. His words wipe in once and hold (41 data-anim-high one-shot wipes; the manifesto at y1800 reads 0% background, 1.27% scroll). Ours do the same.

LIVERY: five constants, so the eye knows it is the same object at 1045px or at 36px.
1. One dark-glass well on the shots' own ground (#1c1a20 to #2b2b2f, decision 32).
2. One radius token.
3. A 1px hairline outline that lights in the accent only while the Screen is in use. This is Lando's helmet card, whose "notched-corner outline lights up lime" on hover (deep pass).
4. The rail's frost caption strip as its one label (`frost` is already default).
5. Something real inside, never a CSS mock (decision 30).

The EA mark is the Screen's signature, written by the PEN (logopen). It is never stamped on the Screen as a logo (decision 24).

FOUR VERBS. Each is a measured Lando device. They are dealt so no two adjacent seams use the same one (grammar law 1).
- PLAY: the Screen moves on its own, only at the two ends of the page.
  - The hero, where Lando's helmet HUD is the only hero motion (about a 3.4s cycle).
  - The close, where his footer strip is still rolling (about 1.3%) as the last moving thing.
  - Between the ends, every picture is still at rest. His wall and helmet grid read 0.00% at rest, and Jake's rule is that evidence imagery stays still.
- BECOME: the Screen arrives larger than its place and contracts into it while its siblings come out from underneath. Three measured sources:
  - Lando's hero shrink into the anchor: power1.inOut over one screen of scroll, plane area 100% to 14.7% (§2.2).
  - The OTOT pair's rate split: images ±266.67 to 0 on (1−p)³, text linear (§2.7).
  - Law 9: the next room is revealed under the current one, already moving.
  - No pin. Jake on the §02 curtain: it "shouldnt be sticky".
- TRAVEL: the Screen, multiplied, rides the page's ONE axis switch. This is Lando's track (§2.5):
  - 1:1 horizontal travel, pre-rolled one viewport so no frame shows a zero state.
  - Each picture drifts only as far as its own surplus (at most about 53px).
  - Captions assemble once by clip wipe.
  - The ground ramps underneath on 2t − t².
- RECEDE then RETURN: the Screen steps back to reveal its own return.
  - Off+Brand's recede, the same studio as Lando: scale 1 to .94 (decision 23).
  - Then Lando's footer (§2.15, law 12): the hero's composition again, a rigid 1:1 rise, one centred object, the signature drawn once more.

ONE HOVER on every still Screen: STILL to IN USE. This is Lando's helmet card: the action shot rises from the bottom edge (0.75s cubic-bezier(.65,.05,0,1) declared, about 90% resolved by 300ms) and the outline lights at the same moment. Ours: the device photo gives way to the site itself, scrolling, using the tall tour captures that already exist. Hover is how a visitor asks a still Screen to play.

THE JOURNEY:
1. PLAY: the hero film.
2. Absent: the poster, the still room. Lando's statement has no helmet in it.
3. BECOME ×3: the three deliverables.
4. Absent: the sentence and doors.
5. TRAVEL ×9: the pinned rail, with paper under it.
6. Holds the clients' words: voices, at the same width on the same axis.
7. Four identical wells at 1:1: runs, only if it stays.
8. RECEDE: the white Screen steps back.
9. RETURN, signed: the same film in the close, and the mark writing itself once.

BUDGET, from Lando's restraint number (6.9% of 1,775 elements ever change a paint property; 78% of those are transforms):
- Per viewport, at most ONE object moving on scroll.
- Transform and opacity only.
- The words are never the moving thing.
- Where there is no Screen in frame, nothing moves on scroll.

The always-on ambient layer belongs to the other directors. The one constraint from this angle: draw it from the object's own geometry, the way Lando's contour lines are his helmet's swirl.
concepts.whyItWowsWithoutStealing:
The census explains why Lando's spectacle never steals: "every moving element is a real, dated photo of him — the spectacle IS the content." This system applies the same rule. Every moving thing is EAS's real work on the one Screen, so motion can't compete with what's being shown; it is what's being shown.

1. One mover per frame. The words wipe once and hold, and the Screen is the only scroll-driven thing in any viewport. The eye has exactly one place to land (Jake's cognitive-ease rule).
2. It moves when it's alone. BECOME contracts while no copy shares the frame. The captions wipe while they are still covered, so they are uncovered already written (laws 3 and 9). Nothing moving ever sits beside a sentence someone is reading, which is exactly why decision 10 removed the old service-shot motion.
3. Still until asked. Between the two ends of the page, every Screen at rest is a still photograph. The only thing that plays mid-page is what a visitor hovers, and what plays is the client's real site scrolling: proof, not decoration.
4. The wow is recognition, not the number of effects.
   - The laptop that played in the hero fills the screen again and splits into three.
   - The nine rail frames are the same object.
   - The clients' words arrive in the same window.
   - The last thing on the page is the first film, signed by the mark writing itself.
   Lando's footer lands because the helmet comes back; this is the same payoff with EAS's own object.

It also answers the gap analysis's root cause directly. The page is a collage of about nine sources that "move in different ways". This system gives every section the same object, the same four verbs and one set of curves, instead of adding a tenth reference.

concepts.name: THE RELAY: choreographed seams
concepts.oneLine: The rooms hold still and the seams move. Every section boundary is one of Lando's measured surface moves, never the same one twice in a row, and it uncovers the next room rather than covering this one. Every word lands once through the one wipe and then holds. At each quiet seam one EAS-owned thing is handed on and keeps moving when you stop: the film, the audiences, the clients, and at the end the mark writing itself.
concepts.theSystem:
ONE RULE GENERATES EVERY SECTION'S MOTION: THE PAGE IS A RELAY OF SEAMS. The rooms are still, the boundaries between them move, and something is always being handed on.

1 · EVERY SEAM IS ONE SURFACE MOVE FROM LANDO'S LEDGER, AND NO MOVE IS USED TWICE IN A ROW. Lando has 10 seams and uses 9 different moves for them (grammar law 1). EAS gets 8 seams and 8 moves:
- S1 THE LEAVE (hero→§02a)
- S2 ARRIVE ON SETTLED GROUND (→show)
- S3 WHITESPACE (→§02b)
- S4 THE AXIS SWITCH + THE ONE GROUND FLIP (→rail)
- S5 RELEASE ON A SETTLED GROUND (→voices)
- S6 THE PLATE (→runs)
- S7 THE FLAP (→objections)
- S8 RECEDE + RISE (→close)

EAS narrows Lando's catalogue in one way, taken from Jake's record: seams UNCOVER and never COVER. He has kept every uncover (the curtain, the Off+Brand recede, paper) and rejected the cover ("services shouldnt rise like that", 2026-09-19). So Lando's sticky-cover climb is left out.

Three more rules apply to every scrubbed seam:
- It pre-rolls one viewport (pivot = top − vh, law 4), so no visible frame shows a zero state.
- The next room is shown under the current one, already moving (law 9).
- Hard in, soft out (law 8).

2 · LOUD AND QUIET SEAMS TAKE TURNS, AND QUIET STRETCHES CARRY A BATON. A seam is either LOUD, where a surface moves with the scroll (S1, S4, S6, S8), or QUIET (S2, S3, S5, S7), and the two alternate (law 7). Every quiet stretch holds a BATON: one element that moves on its own when nothing is scrolled (at least 0.3% of the frame per 500ms). The next seam hands it on:
- the film (hero)
- → the audience strip (§02a/show)
- → the client strip (voices, where §02c folds in as Lando's Partners)
- → the same audience strip along the bottom of the close panel (the bookend).

That matches Lando's own at-rest inventory one for one: the hero glitch cycle (~9%), the message ticker (7–8%), the partners marquee (4.73%) and the footer marquee (~1.3%). His contour field is the medium under all of it. Here the seams declare the field's ink the way his data-gl-change-from/to attributes do, and drawing the field itself belongs to the always-on layer. When scroll motion is loud, nothing runs on its own; when scroll is quiet, something always does. Lando measures exactly this: the photo wall is 32–46% scroll motion with about 0 of its own, and the back third is 8.5% scroll with 7 of 10 stops moving on their own. Only one baton is in view at a time.

3 · WORDS MOVE ONCE. Every block of text enters by the engine's data-wipe, which is already Lando's data-anim-high:
- each line is clipped from inset(0 100% 0 0) to 0 over 600ms, power2.out;
- a cyan bar scales from 1 to 0 starting at +300ms;
- lines are 150ms apart;
- it fires at top 90%, so nobody reads a line mid-wipe, and it fires once.

After that the text never moves again. Lando's statement reads 0% of its own motion and 1.27% scroll motion. The only other moving type on the page is the strips, which are Lando's second type system (the ticker). Text that a seam uncovers is never wiped: the seam's edge is its reveal (decision 27). This retires the other four text styles: leoparpeix's rise, Huge's rotating word and line sweep, and Apple's focus-pull.

4 · STRUCTURE IS A FUNCTION OF SCROLL, CHASED AT 0.1, AND THE GROUND FLIPS ONCE. Structure is computed from scroll position, with the per-effect 0.1 chase on top of Lenis 0.1 (decodes §1). Colour snaps to its value; transforms chase theirs. The page ground flips ONCE, under the one axis switch (paper across the rail, eased 2t−t²). Every later dark room is a panel painted on top of it (law 2): the Runs plate and the close panel. The ground never flips back. There is one pin (the rail), and it sits inside the first ~57% of the page (law 6).

ONE SET OF CURVES:
- linear plus the 0.1 chase for structure
- 2t−t² for the ground
- (1−p)³ for imagery converging (decodes §9)
- power2 for the wipe
- cubic-bezier(.19,1,.22,1) at .6s for every hover (the only curve lando.css ships)

MEASURED TARGETS (same census method):
- Stops that move on their own: from 5/31 now (5/0/0 by thirds) to about 50% of stops from the batons alone (Lando: 16/31 = 52%), spread across all thirds.
- Longest run of stops with nothing moving on its own: from 26 to 6 or fewer. That needs the rail trimmed to Lando's 23% budget and the field under it. Lando's own longest run is 6, in the same place, under his busiest scroll motion.
- Average scroll motion stays about the same (~20%).
- Text entrance styles: 5 → 1.
- Seam moves: 8 of 8 distinct. Ground flips: 1. Pins: 2 → 1.
- Elements that ever change a paint property: 7% or fewer, and at least 75% of those changes are transforms (Lando: 6.9% and 78%).

verdict.answerForJake:
Jake, here's why every version has come up short of Lando's. It isn't how much moves. When you scroll, about a fifth of the screen changes on both sites. The difference is what happens when you stop. His page keeps going: faint lines drift behind everything, a line of words runs under his photo, and a strip rolls under his partners and along the bottom of his footer. On his site, 16 of 31 stops are still moving when you stop scrolling. On yours it's 5, all in the first two screens, then 26 stops in a row where nothing moves. His words never move once they land; the movement is around them. Yours swaps a word on a timer.

The bigger reason is that his site was designed once, as one thing. Yours was built a section at a time, each from a different site you liked. Each piece works on its own. Side by side they read as a collection.

So no more reference sites. We build Lando's quiet layer, one piece at a time, each on its own ?v= link, and measure it against his site with the same script. First come the faint drifting lines behind the whole page. They aren't your logo, because you asked for that out; a version drawn from your mark is there only if you want it. Then a slow line of your audiences under the film, words that land once and stay put, and every button reacting a little. After that: your real site appearing when you hover the work, paper across the work (his lines mostly show on his light section), and your services running along the bottom of the close.
